implementation_notes: Ruby has two actor shapes. Ractor, stdlib since Ruby 3.0, is documented as an actor-model abstraction for thread-safe parallel execution: ractors do not share ordinary objects, messages pass through send/receive, and the GVL is held per ractor so they really run in parallel. concurrent-ruby-edge's Concurrent::Actor is the Erlang/Akka-shaped library: actor classes subclass Concurrent::Actor::Context and implement on_message, only a Reference escapes, tell is fire-and-forget and ask returns a future, and supervision, pools and names come with it. Prefer Ractor for isolation by default on a modern Ruby; prefer Concurrent::Actor when you want supervision trees, references and paths. Messages must be immutable values in both, because anything shared between actors can be mutated concurrently.
code_sketch:
class Counter < Concurrent::Actor::Context
  def initialize(initial) = @count = initial
  def on_message(message) = (@count += message if Integer === message)
end

counter = Counter.spawn(:first, 5)   # returns a Reference, not the actor
counter.tell(1)                      # fire and forget
counter.ask(0).value                 # request/reply -> future
pitfalls: Concurrent::Actor lives in concurrent-ruby-edge, whose documentation warns that edge features may change incompatibly without deprecation; treat the API as unstable.
Under Ractor, ordinary objects cannot be shared: sending an object another ractor still holds raises isolation errors or moves it, so messages must be values.
concurrent-ruby actors run on a shared thread pool by default; a blocking handler starves other actors unless the executor/pool options are chosen deliberately.
A Reference keeps the actor alive through its parent; forgetting terminate! leaks actors.
